We’re going to have 100X more agents in the enterprise working with our data and systems than even people do today. Every AI agent deployment comes down to how successfully they can get access to the critical context to make a decision, do research, or execute tasks. 

90% of the data in an enterprise is unstructured data, which means this critical context is living inside of our documents, contracts, marketing assets, research materials, financial plans, design files, and more. Which means we need effective ways for agents to get access to this critical enterprise content to other work.

We’re excited to partner with NVIDIA to deliver advanced context retrieval -combining lexical and semantic search in Box- to ensure that AI agents can find the most relevant information they’re looking for. All in a way that adheres to their enterprise security, access controls, and data governance policies, so agents only work with the data they’re allowed to.

Great to work with @NVIDIAAI and @JensenHuang on this partnership. Files 🤝 GPUs.

We’re launching VIALS-AA, a leaderboard for Handshake AI’s VIALS benchmark for visual reasoning in life sciences and biotech research

Visual artifacts are central to how scientists analyze experiments and make research decisions, but interpreting them correctly remains a challenge for frontier models. VIALS’ 161 tasks span eight domains and need models to reason over artifacts including gel blots, flow cytometry plots, plasmid maps, and phylogenies. Each task requires models to interpret an artifact and draw a specific scientific conclusion.

We evaluate models by running each task three times in Stirrup, our open source agent harness, with code execution and image inspection tools. GPT-6 Luna (medium) grades each answer against the reference answer, and we report the share of tasks judged correct in all three repeats (pass^3).

Key takeaways:

➤ The top three models are separated by 3 points: Gemini 4 Carbon (high) from @GoogleDeepMind leads narrowly with 64%, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) from @OpenAI at 63% and Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) from @AnthropicAI at 61%

➤ Astra and Sol achieve similar scores to Opus and Sonnet at a much lower Cost per Task: Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) averages $1.64 per task, ~29× as much as Sol (~$0.056). This price difference is significantly driven by turn use - GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) average ~8 turns per task, compared with ~27 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) and ~25 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback)

➤ Open weights models trail the highest score by ~19 points: Kimi K3.1 Pro leads open weights models on VIALS-AA at 45%, narrowly ahead of MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 43%

➤ 14 of 161 tasks saw safety refusals on at least one model: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) refused on 6 tasks, the most of any model, and half of the 14 affected tasks saw refusals from multiple models

Thank you to @joinHandshakeAI and the VIALS authors for creating the benchmark and collaborating with us on bringing it to Artificial Analysis!

Launching Artificial Analysis Endpoint Accuracy Index v1.1: a minor version upgrade alongside expanded coverage for GLM-5.3 Flash and Muse Spark Open. Across the 100+ serverless endpoints we benchmarked, nearly 1 in 4 score below the reference

Providers trade off accuracy to optimize for speed and cost. They quantize weights, write custom kernels, tune their inference stacks and cap output lengths, and sometimes they simply ship bugs. The Endpoint Accuracy Index measures how much of a model’s accuracy each endpoint preserves, so developers can pick providers on accuracy, not just price and speed.

We score each endpoint as a percentage of our self-hosted reference deployment of the official weights, across tool calling (BFCL-500), scientific reasoning (HLE-250) and long context recall (AA-LCR-25), equally weighted.

What’s changed:

➤ Upgraded AA-LCR-25 to AA-LCR v1.1 and increased repeats from 10 to 25: AA-LCR v1.1 corrects errors and ambiguities in answer keys and moves grading to GPT-5.6 Luna (medium). Running each question 25 times, up from 10, reduces the average 95% confidence interval from ±4.7 to ±2.6 points

➤ Expanded coverage to six open weights models: We add GLM-5.3 Flash (max) and Meta’s Muse Spark Open (xhigh), alongside DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max), GLM-5.3 (max), Kimi K3 (max) and gpt-oss-120b (high)

Key takeaways for GLM-5.3 Flash:

➤ 16 of 22 endpoints are statistically in line with the reference, and one scores above it (104.2)

➤ Output token caps limit the model on complex workloads: Two endpoints capped at ~32K output tokens cut off about half of HLE-250 responses before an answer, scoring 22% and 29% against 55% for the reference

➤ Endpoints that reason less give lower quality answers: Two endpoints produce ~30% fewer reasoning tokens than the reference on HLE-250, with no truncation, and score 48% against 55%

Key takeaways for Muse Spark Open:

➤ Three of five endpoints match the reference: They score 99.5 to 99.9, including one serving FP4 weights

➤ The other two lose accuracy only on tool calling: Both return tool arguments that the tool defines as text, such as booking IDs, as numbers, scoring 50% and 51% on BFCL-500 against 59%. On HLE-250 and AA-LCR-25 they are within 2 points of the reference

In AA-PersonalityBench, Qwen3.8 27B writes the longest responses of any model measured, averaging about 1,030 words, roughly 6x as long as GPT-6 Sol at 174 words

Average response length varies widely across the models measured, from 174 words to about 1,030 words for the same questions.

Average words per response:

➤ Longest: Qwen3.8 27B (1,030), K2 Horizon 375B A23B (922), Qwen3.8 Max (0902) (863), Muse Spark Open (809) and Gemini 4 Argon (790)

➤ Shortest: GPT-6 Sol (174), GPT-3.5 Turbo (180), GPT-6 Luna (270), GPT-6.1 Sol (337) and GPT-6 Astra (352)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash speeds on GB300 NVL72 have increased by up to 1.5x tok/s per agent over the past month on AA-AgentPerf, our benchmark of datacenter systems running realistic agentic coding workloads

This improvement comes from a newer vLLM version, new vLLM kernels for DeepSeek V4.1 on GB300, FlashInfer autotuning, fuller CUDA graph coverage, tuned speculative decoding, and running prefill and decode on the same GPUs in NVIDIA’s updated Dynamo + vLLM setup

➤ Faster speeds: 848 tok/s for a single agent, up from 596 (1.42x)

➤ Higher throughput: ~1.6x the throughput per GPU at ~80 tok/s per agent

We will all be learning in coming weeks & months, that most human-made software:

▫️ Was really slow
▫️ Had many security vulnerabilities

AI will rewrite it all. Many times. It will make it fast, cost-efficient, and secure. It will think about failure modes we couldn't wrap our heads around.

In many ways, we are witnessing the true birth of software engineering.

tweets.text: I am a broken record about this, but: frontier agents are not going to be a purely digital phenomenon for much longer. They will be able to use anything in the physical world that can be actuated programmatically—first competently, then at human-expert level, then superhuman. By and large, we probably won’t need specialist models; the frontier models will just do it. If your model of the future hinges on physical AI happening “for real” many years into the future, I think you will be in for a surprise.

Voters delivered an overwhelming message on data centers this week, and it is incumbent upon industry actors to hear that message and respond to it by building AI infrastructure in ways that benefit both individual communities and the country as a whole.

Astra is one of my favorite technology releases of all time and I’d be saying that regardless of whether I worked at OpenAI. In fact, if I didn’t work at OpenAI, I’d surely be talking about how wonderful I find Astra much more.
